## Methods

Animals
Laboratory Animal Medical Services (LAMS), Animal Care and Use Program (ACUP) and the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) are housed at the University of Cincinnati. All animal protocols were approved by IACUC. Approved animal protocol number is 24-02-27-01. Within LAMS, mice are held to a 14 h light/10 h dark cycle. NestinCreER (JAX:016261)59 and Ai9R26-CAG-tdTomato (JAX:007909)105 were used to endogenously label and track NSCs. We generated cell-type-specific inducible knockout models of critical TGF-β signaling components using Cx3cr1CreER(Jung) (JAX:020940)53, Cx3cr1CreER(Littman) (JAX:021160)54, and P2ry12CreER (JAX:034727)58, to delete Alk5, Tgfbr2, Igf1 in microglia or Tnfα constitutive knockout. Alk5 (JAX:028701)106 floxed or Tgfbr2 (JAX:012603)107 floxed mice, and Tnfα KO (JAX:005540)108 and Igf1 floxed (JAX:016831)109 mice were crossed with Cx3cr1CreER(Jung), all purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. We crossed the above microglia CreER lines with ROSA26-YFP (JAX:006148)110 in some of the experiments to facilitate microglia sorting. All animals were euthanized by administration of avertin (2.5%) followed by transcardial perfusion with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) (for IHC) or 1x HBSS (for FACS, RNAseq, and qRT-PCR) as previously described36. Mice were bred on a C57BL/6J background and both sexes were used in all experiments. All animals were used unless tissue quality was poor as a result of subpar perfusions or inadequate cryoprotection. For all experiments, bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) was administered intraperitoneally at 100mg/kg per injection (10µl/g bodyweight, Invitrogen #000103) during the indicated time frame in each experimental timeline and harvested between 3-12 weeks post-TAM.

Tamoxifen administration
3 or 5 consecutive gavage injections of TAM (specified in each experiment/figure) solution were given to 6-16-week-old male and female mice, administered at a dosage of 180mg/kg. 900µL of sunflower seed oil and 100µL of ethanol were sonicated with 30mg of TAM powder protected from light36. To evaluate the effect of microglia-mediated TGF-β signaling silencing in adult neurogenesis, young adult mice were harvested at 3, 6-, or 12-weeks post-TAM to evaluate microglia phenotype and SGZ neurogenesis.

Microglia ablation PLX5622
Mice were given either the control diet (Plexxikon) or PLX5622 diet (Plexxikon) as previously described36,111 for the duration of the study. All animals had unrestricted access to diet and water. For studying the phenotype of homeostatic microglia on baseline adult neurogenesis, we administered TAM to NestinCreER-Ai9 mice to label a NSCs and their progeny, followed by 3 weeks of control or PLX5622 diet. Mice were harvested 3 weeks post-TAM and brains were harvested for IHC staining. For assessing the role of repopulating Alk5 KO microglia in the stimulation of adult neurogenesis, mice were treated with a control PLX5622 diet for 3 weeks, followed by TAM treatment during the last 3 days. These animals were then switched to a standard chow diet to allow the repopulation of WT or Alk5 KO microglia over the course of 3 weeks, when they were harvested by administration of avertin (2.5%) followed by transcardial perfusion with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Brain tissue was harvested for IHC staining.

Fluorescent activated cell sorting (FACS)
Mice were harvested by administration of avertin (2.5%) followed by transcardial perfusion with cold 1x HBSS for 3–4 mins before the brain was extracted. The brains were mechanically dissociated via a scalpel before enzymatically dissociated with the papain dissociation system (9001-73-4, Worthington Biochemical Corporation) while all of the above processes are carried out in the presence of transcriptional and translational inhibitors to prevent microglial gene expression changes during the isolation protocol60. Once the brain is sufficiently dissociated, 37% percoll solution was used to clear any excess myelin or debris. Cells were resuspended in FACS buffer (0.5% BSA in PBS) for staining and sorting using a BD/FACSAria II (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ). CD11b, CD45, and GFP reporter were used to develop a gating strategy to enrich microglia. Sorted microglial cells were used for qRT-PCR or bulk RNAseq for gene expression analysis as described below.

qRT-PCR
Using the RNAqueous-Micro Total RNA isolation kit (AM1931, Thermo Fisher Scientific), RNA was isolated from sorted microglia as previously described36. Supercript III reverse transcriptase (18080044, Thermo Fisher Scientific) or iScript cDNA synthesis kit (1708890, BioRad) was used to generate cDNA. Following cDNA synthesis, qRT-PCR probes Hmbs1 (hydroxymethylbilane synthase), Hprt1 (hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase 1), Aif1, Alk5, Igf1, Tnf, Tmem119, and P2ry12 were used to analyze cDNA levels using a Roche LightCycler II 480. Relative gene expression was calculated using the ΔΔCt method compared to Hmbs1 as a reference gene and expressed as fold change compared to the average of control cells for each individual gene.

Immunohistochemistry
Mice were anesthetized with avertin (2.5%), then perfused with 4% PFA. The brains were harvested and post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight. In the following days, brains were switched to 20% and 30% sucrose respectively until brains sank. Each brain was sectioned at 30µM thickness on a cryostat and used for immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining as previously described36. Antibodies for BrdU (1:500, Abcam), DCX (1:1000, Cell Signaling), Ki67 (1:500, Invitrogen), IBA1 (1:1000, Abcam), TMEM119 (1:2000, GeneTex), P2RY12 (1:200, Biolegend), GFAP (1:1000, Sigma), pSMAD3 (1:200, Abcam), beta-3 tubulin (1:2000, Promega), pS6 (1:800, Cell Signaling), Olig2 (1:500, R&D Systems), MBP (1:250, Biorad), NG2 (1:500, Millipore) were used. P2RY12 clone: P2YM 17A12112 (1:500), and P2RY12 clone: P2YM 1E5112 (1:500) was generated and validated as previously described. Brain sections were blocked for 1h at room temperature in 4% BSA/0.3% Triton-x100 and incubated in primary antibody solution (diluted in blocking buffer) on a shaker overnight at 4°C. Secondary antibodies conjugated with Alexa fluorescence 488, 555, 647 or 790 (1:500) were incubated with the brain sections for 4 hours at room temperature. Confocal imaging of stained brain sections was carried out using a Leica Stellaris 8. Quantification of cell counts was carried out using ImageJ (1.53) software. At least 3 coronal sections with the respective region of interest were quantified for each mouse and averaged to be used as a single data point.

BrdU Immunohistochemistry
Animals injected with BrdU labeling reagent (10µl/g bodyweight, Invitrogen #000103) at various time points after injection were harvested following avertin (2.5%) injection and PB/PFA perfusion. As described previously113, coronal or sagittal cryosections were washed 3x at RT and incubated in pre-warmed freshly made DNA denaturation solution (50% formamide, 50% 2x SSC buffer) for 2 hours at 60°C with shaking. After being washed 3x in 2x SSC at 60°C with shaking, the tissue was incubated in 2N HCl at 37°C with shaking. Then, the sections were incubated 1x in borate buffer (pH 8.5) at RT with shaking for 10 min and washed 1x in PB at RT. The tissue was blocked in blocking buffer for 1h at RT and the standard immunofluorescent protocol was followed (see Immunohistochemistry above).

scRNAseq
Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed at Single Cell Discoveries (https://www.scdiscoveries.com/) according to the 10x Genomics Single Cell Gene Expression Flex solution protocol. Mice were anesthetized with avertin (2.5%), then perfused with 1x PB before whole hippocampal pieces were micro-dissected from the brain and flash-frozen on dry ice. Samples were shipped on dry ice to Single Cell Discoveries where all Processing of samples was performed by Single Cell sequencing experts. For each sample, 8000–14,000 cells were loaded and sequencing libraries were prepared following a standard 10x Genomics protocol.
As similarly described by others114, sample reads were aligned to the mouse genome GRCm39 (Datasets - 10x Genomics) using Cell Ranger 9.0.0 Flex pipeline (Flex with Cell Ranger multi-Official 10x Genomics Support). The data from all samples were loaded in R (version 4.3.2) and processed using the Seurat package (5.1.0). Cells expressing least 200 genes and less than 20% mitochondrial gene content were retained for analysis. The data of all 10x libraries was merged and processed together and normalized for sequencing depth per cell and log transformed. After data cleaning and filtering, datasets were integrated using Harmony115. Following this, clustering was done using the FindNeighbors function (dims=1:20) at a resolution of 0.12. To identify cell types in separate clusters, signature genes for each cell type were used based on the Cell Marker 2.0 database for mouse species in brain tissue. To analyze differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between control and MG-Alk5 or MG-Tgfb1 iKO samples, we used FindMarkers to filter for genes that were expressed in at least 10% of cells in either of the conditions and had an adjusted p-value of <0.05. DEGs from either neuroblast or microglia cluster were plotted onto a volcano plot using R packages DESeq2 and EnhancedVolcano. These DEGs were input into EnrichR for pathway enrichment analysis. Intercellular signaling was profiled using LIANA (v0.2.0). LIANA aggregated predictions from multiple computational methods (including CellPhoneDB, NATMI, SCA and LogFc) and ranked interactions based on the consensus mean rank score. The Mouse Consensus ligand–receptor database was used as the reference resource. Visualization of significant ligand–receptor pairs was generated using ggplot2 based on LIANA’s aggregated output.

Rapamycin treatment
To evaluate the contributions of mTOR signaling on adult neurogenesis after deletion of microglia-mediated ALK5 signaling, control or MG-Alk5 iKO mice received TAM for 5 days to delete Alk5 in microglia. Daily intraperitoneal (I.P.) injections of rapamycin were given starting from the 4th day of TAM for 21 days to 4-6-month-old male and female mice, administered at a dosage of 10mg/kg similar to previous studies96,98. 5% PEG 400 and 5% Tween 80 was diluted into MQH2O with 4% rapamycin (diluted in EtOH) or 4% EtOH to generate a working solution of 1mg/mL. Mice were harvested 3 weeks post-TAM by administering avertin (2.5%) and then transcardially perfused with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA).

Tissue culture
Isolation of primary adult neural stem cells (aNSCs) from C57B6 WT mice is established as previously described5. Mice (6-week-old) were culled by cervical dislocation, and the SVZ was microdissected and dissociated into single cells. Adult NSCs are cultured with neurobasal media containing heparin, EGF, bFGF, and B-27 as described in our previous studies5,116,117. Single cells are cultured as neurospheres in the media above. Neurospheres between passages 5 and 7 were used for in vitro experiments where the disassociated single cells were plated at 3×10^3 cells/well in a ultra-low attachment 96-well round-bottom plate. These aNSCs were then given 5 days to form a sphere and proliferate before co-cultured with primary mouse microglia (mMG). The mMG used was obtained from P3 pups with a P2ry12CreERT/CreERT2-Alk5WT/WT or P2ry12CreERT2/CreERT2-Alk5fl/fl genotype via a mixed glial culture of the whole brain (excluding the olfactory bulb and cerebellum). The tissue collected and processed were put into a poly-D-lysine coated T75 flask with one flask per pup in glial media (DMEM/F-12, 10% FBS, 1% 100X L-Glutamate, 1% Pen/Strep). Feeds consisting of glial media were given every 3 days. On day 11, the flasks were given 1μM 4-OH TAM diluted in ethanol. On day 14, the flasks were then fed with glial media and shaken on an orbital shaker at 180 rpm for 3 h to collect WT or KO mMG. Alk5 mRNA decrease in the KO mMG was confirmed by qRT-PCR. The collected WT or KO mMG (3000 cells per sphere) was added to the NSC neutrospheres to establish the 3D co-culture. 3 days after the microglia were added to the neurospheres, the media were changed to differentiation media consisting of neurobasal media without growth factors but with microglia serum (from ScienCell’s microglia medium) to help maintain the microglia while differentiating the aNSCs. Additionally, 100 nM rapamycin or vehicle (ethanol) was added to the differentiation media. The co-culture was then differentiated for 4 days before fixation via 4% PFA. The fixed co-culture spheres were then stained by permeabilizing them via 0.3% 100X Triton in DPBS for 10 minutes, blocked with blocking buffer (4% BSA/0.3% 100X Triton) for 1 hour, incubated in primary antibody solution (βIII-Tubulin [1:2000, Promega] and GFAP [1:1000, BioLegend]) for 4 days at 4C, washed with DPBS 4x, incubated in secondary antibodies (Donkey anti-Mouse 647 [1:500, Jackson ImmunoResearch] and Donkey anti-rabbit 488+ [1:1000, Invitrogen]) and DAPI diluted in blocking buffer for 3 days at 4C, and washed 4x for 5 mins each. Neurospheres were then imaged using a Leica Stellaris 8 confocal microscope and quantified in ImageJ for % area of immunoreactivity.

Behavioral tests
EPM/EZM. Elevated Plus Maze (EPM) or Elevated Zero Maze (EZM) was used to assess anxiety-like behavior in mice. The EPM or EZM is elevated ~60 cm off the floor. The EPM consists of a cross-shaped platform that is 5cm wide and 30cm long with two opposing arms containing dark walls that are 15cm high. The EZM is an O-ring-shaped platform that is 60cm in diameter with a 5cm wide platform. Two sections of the O-shaped apparatus are enclosed by dark walls 15cm high. Black-out curtains surround the testing area to help maintain a consistent lighting of 18 lux via LED strips45. Animals are habituated to the room for at least 20 minutes before testing. In between each animal, the apparatus is cleaned with warm water and 10% Conflikt (Decon Labs). Each animal is allowed to freely explore the apparatus for 5 minutes before being returned to their home cage. EPM is the first behavioral test, and for the second anxiety test, EZM is used to prevent repeated exposure to the same maze. Data was automatically scored using AnyMaze (Stoelting Company, Wood Dale, IL).

Barnes maze. To evaluate spatial learning and memory in mice, the Barnes Maze apparatus (Stoelting Company, Wood Dale, IL) was used as previously described36. Using a short and challenging paradigm, we trained the animals in two separate sessions 4h apart where the animals were motivated to locate the escape hole during each session with light and a fan. Animals were tested the following day. In between each animal, the apparatus was cleaned with warm water followed by 20% ethanol and allowed to dry. Data was automatically scored using AnyMaze (Stoelting Company, Wood Dale, IL).

Rotarod. Motor coordination and motor learning were assessed in animals using the Roto-rod Series 8 apparatus (IITC Life Science Inc., Woodland Hills, CA) with an acceleration paradigm starting at 5 rpm and reaching a maximum of 20 rpm over 300 seconds. Once each animal reached the end of the 300 seconds or fell off the rotating rod, they were returned to their cages after 3 consecutive trials with rest in between. The Roto-rod apparatus was sanitized using 70% ethanol in between each animal.

Quantification and statistical analysis
All data were analyzed using SigmaPlot (12.0) for statistical significance. Results are expressed by mean±SEM of the indicated number of experiments. Statistical analysis was performed using the two-sided Student’s t-test, two-sided Welch’s t-test, and two-sided one- or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), as appropriate, with Tukey’s post hoc tests. A p-value to or less than 0.05 was considered significant. When the data did not meet the assumptions of normality or equal variance, the corresponding nonparametric tests were used. The significance level was set at α=0.05. Number of animals used in each experiment plotted as single data point and are indicated in Figure legends. Graphs were made in GraphPad Prism (10.6.1) and portions of figures were created with BioRender.com. The notation for p-values was as follows: n.s – p≥0.05, * – p<0.05, ** – p<0.01, *** – p<0.001, **** – p<0.0001.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript by Ware and colleagues investigated the role of microglia in subgranular zone neurogenesis in adult microglia-specific Tgfb1- and Tgfbr1-deficient mice. The authors convincingly demonstrated that Tgfb1- and Tgfbr1-deficient mice develop dyshomeostatic microglia (as previously shown by the same group) resulting in transiently increased neurogenesis in the hippocampal subgranular zone which was accompanied by altered anxiety-like behaviour. Using elegant transgenic models and BrdU injections, the authors revealed that enhanced survival and not proliferation of DCX+ cells is essential for the observed increased adult neurogenis in the presence of Alk5-deficient microglia. Depletion of microglia did not result in increased neurogenesis but repopulation with Alk5-deficient microglia increased adult neurogenesis. Moreover, using scRNAseq, the authors identified reduced PTEN signaling in new born neuroblasts and reversed the transiently heightened neurogenesis by rapamicycin-induced mTOR signaling inhibition. Overall, the study is well designed, well structured, and the results are presented with high quality figures. Together, the study provides valuable data which further broadens the knowledge of microglia-regulated hippocampal adult neurogenesis and highlights the essential role of microglial TGF-beta signaling.

The authors should address the following points to further strengthen the overall message of the current manuscript.
- The authors should demonstrate that Cre-mediated Alk5 ablation permanently affects microglia and recovers in peripheral monocytes/macrophages. Are BAMS affected in the same way as microglia?
- Igf1 upregulation was linked to adult neurogenesis. Igf1-positive microglia have also been described to drive oligodendrocyte differentiation during postnatal development. Has the number of mature and immature oligodendrocytes been analysed? Is the myelination affected in Alk5 deficient mice?
- The authors observed increases in DCX+ cells at 3 weeks but not by 6 and 12 weeks post tamoxifen treatment. However, the microglia phenotypes have only been analysed after 3 weeks (Fig.1). Do microglia at 6 and 12 weeks show the same phenotype at 6 and 12 weeks?
- Experimental schemes in all figures should by consistent (see Fig.1A vs. Fig.3A)
- DCX+ cells as well as the dendrite arborization has been analysed only in P2ry12Cre/Alk5 hippocampi. Why was the dendrite arborization not addressed in Cx3cr1Cre/Alk5 mice?
- The overall story would extremely benefit from data showing spine density (Golgi staining) and/or levels of pre and postsynaptic markers such as synapsin and PSD95 (via IHC or western blot)
- During the depletion experiments (Fig.5) DCX+ cells were analyzed after 12 weeks. According to Fig.2, numbers of DCX+ cells were only increased after 3 weeks in Alk5-deficient mice. Why were the numbers of DCX+ cells analysed 3 weeks and 6 weeks after microglia depletion? Without this information it is difficult to state that microglia depletion has no effect on adult neurogenesis.
- Although the authors have convincingly demonstrated that Igf1 as well as Tnfa (as evidenced by substantial supplementary material including Alk5/Igf1 and Alk5/Tnfa dKO mice data) are not the key players driving increased adult neurogenesis, other neurotrophic factors could be involved and should be part of the discussion.
- For the behaviour experiments, mice received a different TAM regime as in all other parts of the study. Why has that approach been chosen and not applied to all other experimental parts?
- Elevated zero maze data are not presented for Alk5-defeicient mice. Why? Moroever, why is the number of mice analyzed for EZM so low compared to all other tests?

Overall, the manuscript contains very interesting data describing increased adult neurogenesis in microglia-specific TGFb-signalling and TGFb1 deficient mice. Next to the abovementioned points, the story would substantially improve if data on synaptic densities, microglial synapric pruning will be added. Spine density (Golgi staining) and/or levels of pre and postsynaptic markers such as synapsin and PSD95 (via IHC or western blot) as well uptake of synaptic material by microglia (either IHC or flow cytomtrey) should be added.

### Reviewer 2

Summary
This potentially interesting study investigates the role of TGF-β signaling in microglia and its impact on adult hippocampal neurogenesis and behavior. The authors use inducible knockout models targeting various TGF-β pathway components (e.g., Alk5, Tgfbr2, Tgfb1) specifically in microglia. They report that disruption of TGF-β signaling leads to microglial dyshomeostasis, increased proliferation and survival of adult-born neurons in the subgranular zone, and altered anxiety-like and cognitive behavior. scRNA-seq and pharmacological interventions suggest this effect is mediated via downregulation of PTEN and activation of the mTOR pathway in neuroblasts. The findings suggest that activated microglia can stimulate adult neurogenesis and modulate affective and cognitive behavior, but they do not demonstrate this directly. Additional experiments are needed to establish a causal link. Furthermore, more thorough analyses of the histological data, the animal models, and sex of mice are needed.

Major Comments:
1. Although both Cx3cr1CreER and P2ry12CreER drivers are used, the reliance on Cx3cr1CreER raises concerns about off-target recombination in BAMs and peripheral myeloid cells. Additional validation using BAM-specific markers or region-specific analysis (e.g., meninges, choroid plexus) would strengthen the microglia-specific conclusions.
2. The degree of Alk5 deletion and recombination efficiency at the protein level is not shown. Demonstrating this with IHC or Western blot for ALK5 in sorted microglia would reinforce the mechanistic link to TGF-β signaling loss.
3. The study concludes that TNF-α and IGF-1 are not responsible for the observed increase in neurogenesis. However, given known redundancy and interplay in cytokine signaling, additional discussion or testing of combinatorial cytokine blockade would be important.
4. Rapamycin only partially rescues the adult neurogenesis phenotype. This suggests that alternative or parallel pathways might be involved. Additional discussion is needed to address the possibility of other downstream signals in activated microglia.
5. While the manuscript demonstrates increased adult neurogenesis following TGF-β signaling disruption in microglia, the causal molecular mechanism remains underdeveloped. The study eliminates IGF-1 and TNF-α as single factors and implicates the PTEN/mTOR, it does not explore whether the changes in PTEN/mTOR in neuroblasts are a direct result of microglial-derived cues (e.g., cytokines).
6. The authors report reduced avoidance behavior in the EPM and diminished cognitive performance on the Barnes maze in microglial TGF-β iKO mice but cannot attribute this directly to increased adult neurogenesis. Without this important connection, it is impossible to interpret the microglia effects as working through changes in adult born neurons. This possibility could be assessed by blocking adult neurogenesis in the MG-Alk5-iKO during the behavioral testing window.
7. The cell count data are presented per section or per image field. This type of analysis can lead to inaccurate comparisons if the brain regions of different treatment groups differ in size/volume. The data should be presented as overall counts in a given brain region or as cell densities (number of cells per volume).
8. The n size varies greatly across experiments. What is the justification for this? In cases where just 3 mice are analyzed, it is questionable whether reliable results will be obtained. Also, some of the data are presented with points representing individual cells. This is misleading and the data should be shown as points for individual mice.
9. The distribution of males and females is not even across the studies. Did the authors investigate whether trends toward sex differences exist? If not, it is difficult to compare across measures when some of them have with mixed sex mice and others have only one sex (e.g., Figure 4H).
10. Avoidance behavior on the EPM has been linked to ventral hippocampus, not dorsal hippocampus. The images are all from dorsal hippocampus and it is not clear whether the entire hippocampus was analyzed or just the dorsal part. Ventral hippocampus should be included.
11. Terms like "microglial activation," "dyshomeostasis," and "reactivity" are used interchangeably. Consider defining and using them more consistently for clarity. It is not clear at all what microglial dyshomeostasis is. Unless there is something different from microglial reactivity, it should be eliminated from the text. If there is something different, it should be defined as such.
12. The authors note that increased adult neurogenesis is transient (DCX+ peaks at 3 weeks). Discussion on whether this reflects compensatory regulatory feedback, or microglia reversion to a homeostatic state might be helpful. Whether changes in neurogenesis correlate with sustained changes in microglial profile (e.g., do activated microglia persist at 6–12 weeks?).

### Reviewer 4

This manuscript investigates the consequences of microglia-specific TGF-β signaling inhibition on hippocampal adult neurogenesis and behavior. Using multiple inducible knockout models (targeting TGF-β1, ALK5, and TβRII), the authors demonstrate that loss of microglial homeostatic signaling leads to a transient increase in SGZ neurogenesis and a lasting increase in mature neurons. Single-cell RNA sequencing and pharmacological inhibition experiments support a mechanistic link via downregulation of PTEN and upregulation of the mTOR pathway in neuroblasts. Behavioral testing indicates reduced anxiety-like behavior but no alteration in forgetting.

This work is conceptually innovative, methodologically rigorous, and highly relevant for the fields of neurogenesis, microglia-neuron crosstalk, and neuroinflammation. However, clarification and strengthening of mechanistic interpretation, figure presentation, and behavioral conclusions would improve the manuscript.

Major Comments
1. The finding that activated microglia can stimulate, rather than inhibit, adult neurogenesis in the absence of injury contradicts longstanding assumptions and presents a paradigm shift.
2. The integration of transcriptomic and behavioral data makes this study of broad relevance to neuroscience and regenerative biology.
3. The authors argue that the observed transient increase in DCX+ neuroblasts results in a long-term gain in mature neurons. While this is supported by BrdU/NeuN data, the term "transient" may be misleading. Please clarify this distinction and emphasize that the transient increase refers to proliferation/differentiation, not integration.
4. The PTEN-mTOR link is well-supported; however, the authors should discuss whether other converging pathways from their DEG data (e.g., synaptic organization, apoptotic signaling) might also contribute.
5. Behavioral phenotypes (reduced anxiety-like behavior and spatial learning deficits) are presented as consequences of increased neurogenesis. However, causality remains correlative. While the authors acknowledge limitations, the discussion would benefit from more elaboration on future strategies to test this directly (e.g., combining NSC-targeted inhibition with microglial KO background).
6. The fear-conditioning “forgetting” paradigm might not be ideally timed. Consider clarifying whether pre-treatment with TAM would be more suitable to test the influence of neurogenesis on memory clearance.
7. The Barnes Maze was used to assess spatial learning, but reversal learning—a component of cognitive flexibility strongly linked to adult hippocampal neurogenesis—was not tested. Given prior work by Kempermann and others demonstrating that reversal learning in tasks like the Morris Water Maze is sensitive to neurogenesis status, the authors should briefly discuss this limitation or provide justification for the behavioral test battery selected.
8. The scRNA-seq data are rich, but dense. Please consider a summary table or schematic of key pathway-level changes (PTEN/mTOR, IGF1, TNF-α) for clarity.
9. Improve visual clarity of UMAPs and volcano plots (Figure 7), including font sizes, axis labels, and color keys.
10. Some experiments (e.g., PLX5622 repopulation) use n=3–4 animals. These data should be interpreted cautiously, and limitations of statistical power noted.
11. Sex as a variable and tamoxifen effects: The inclusion of both sexes and annotation of data points by sex across figures is commendable. However, no sex-specific analysis is reported. If the study was not powered or intended to detect sex differences, please state this explicitly in the Methods or Discussion sections.
Additionally, tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), and estrogen signaling differs between males and females—particularly in the hippocampus where it influences both neurogenesis and microglial function. Although tamoxifen is used here solely for Cre activation, the potential for sex-dependent off-target effects should be acknowledged, especially when interpreting behavioral and neurogenic outcomes.

Minor Comments
12. Figure 7K–N: Highlight DCX+ cells migrating out of SGZ more clearly with arrows or labels.
13. Clarify whether the scRNA-seq was done on the whole hippocampus or DG-specific regions.
14. Refer consistently to “dyshomeostatic microglia” or “TGF-β-deficient microglia” rather than broadly as “activated microglia.”

microglia. They report that disruption of TGF-β signaling leads to microglial dyshomeostasis,
increased proliferation and survival of adult-born neurons in the subgranular zone, and altered
anxiety-like and cognitive behavior. scRNA-seq and pharmacological interventions suggest this
effect is mediated via downregulation of PTEN and activation of the mTOR pathway in
neuroblasts. The findings suggest that activated microglia can stimulate adult neurogenesis and
modulate affective and cognitive behavior, but they do not demonstrate this directly. Additional
experiments are needed to establish a causal link. Furthermore, more thorough analyses of the
histological data, the animal models, and sex of mice are needed.
Major Comments:
1. Although both Cx3cr1CreER and P2ry12CreER drivers are used, the reliance on
Cx3cr1CreER raises concerns about off-target recombination in BAMs and peripheral myeloid
cells. Additional validation using BAM-specific markers or region-specific analysis (e.g.,
meninges, choroid plexus) would strengthen the microglia-specific conclusions.
- We have now added data to show that peripheral myeloid cells are not affected in the
Cx3cr1CreER Alk5 iKO mice (New Supplemental Fig 1), consistent with our previous
report in the Cx3cr1CreER Tgfb1 iKO mice (PMID: 38906887). Additionally, we
quantified the pSMAD signal in microglia, perivascular macrophages, and choroid plexus
macrophages in both the Cx3cr1CreER and P2ry12CreER/CreER Alk5 iKO mice (New
Supplemental Fig 7). Interestingly, both perivascular macrophages and choroid plexus
macrophages show reduced pSMAD3 signaling in the Cx3cr1CreER mice. In the P2ry12
CreER Alk5 iKO mice, microglia show partial pSMAD3 loss compared to Cx3cr1CreER
Alk5 iKO microglia, consistent with the lower recombination efficiency of this mouse
line. Perivascular macrophages show similar pSMAD3 levels, and choroid plexus
macrophages show reduced pSMAD3 levels, consistent with the previous report of the
lack of reporter recombination in perivascular macrophages but presence of
recombination in choroid plexus macrophages (PMID 32573436 and 38217856). Based
on this data, we have now revised the results and discussion to reflect that the phenotype
of increased DCX+ cells might be due to changes in parenchymal microglia and/or
choroid plexus macrophages.
2. The degree of Alk5 deletion and recombination efficiency at the protein level is not shown.
Demonstrating this with IHC or Western blot for ALK5 in sorted microglia would reinforce the
mechanistic link to TGF-β signaling loss.
- We were not able to validate any good antibody for ALK5 via Western blot or
immunostaining (using WT and constitutive Alk5 KO tissue), therefore, we used the
downstream signaling effector of the Alk5 receptor, phosphorylation of SMAD3
(pSMAD3) as a readout for ALK5-mediated TGF-β signaling. We have now provided
data on pSMAD3 staining in the Alk5 and Tgfb1iKO lines at 3, 6 and 12 weeks post TAM
(New Supplemental Fig 3 and 6).
3. The study concludes that TNF-α and IGF-1 are not responsible for the observed increase in
neurogenesis. However, given known redundancy and interplay in cytokine signaling, additional
discussion or testing of combinatorial cytokine blockade would be important.
- We have revised our conclusion to be that increased TNF-α or IGF1 in the iKO microglia
is not necessary for the observed increase in neurogenesis. The results on Igf1 KO are
consistent with a recent publication showing that in humans, microglia-derived IGF1 is
critical for interneuron neurogenesis, which is not recapitulated in mice (PMID
40770097). There might be species differences at play here. Nevertheless, we have now
added more discussion on combinatorial effects of growth factors as well as redundancy
and interplay in cytokine signaling (pages 17, 24-25).
4. Rapamycin only partially rescues the adult neurogenesis phenotype. This suggests that
alternative or parallel pathways might be involved. Additional discussion is needed to address
the possibility of other downstream signals in activated microglia.
- Rapamycin in vivo treatment completely rescues the adult neurogenesis phenotype in the
measurements of DCX+ cells and dendrite arborization (no difference was observed
between the WT and KO in the rapamycin-treated group). Rapamycin shows an effect of
its own on the migration of these cells in the DG. Our new in vitro experiments of the 3D
co-culture of WT NSC with WT or Alk5 KO microglia show a similar phenotype in
differentiated immature neurons, which is also reversed by Rapamycin treatment (New
Fig. 9).
5. While the manuscript demonstrates increased adult neurogenesis following TGF-β signaling
disruption in microglia, the causal molecular mechanism remains underdeveloped. The study
eliminates IGF-1 and TNF-α as single factors and implicates the PTEN/mTOR, it does not
explore whether the changes in PTEN/mTOR in neuroblasts are a direct result of microglial-
derived cues (e.g., cytokines).
- We now show increased mTOR signaling (measured by downstream signaling pS6) in
DCX+ neuroblasts in vivo in the MG Alk5 iKO mice, and Rapamycin treatment abolishes
this increase in iKO mice (New Fig 9). We also show directly that coculture of KO
microglia with WT neuroblasts increased the neuronal differentiation in NSC 3D co-
culture system compared to co-culture with WT MG. This phenotype is also rescued by
rapamycin treatment in the iKO coculture, while neuronal differentiation is not affected
in the WT coculture (New Fig 9), demonstrating that microglia-derived cues acting on the
mTOR pathway are causally linked to this phenotype.
6. The authors report reduced avoidance behavior in the EPM and diminished cognitive
performance on the Barnes maze in microglial TGF-β iKO mice but cannot attribute this directly
to increased adult neurogenesis. Without this important connection, it is impossible to interpret
the microglia effects as working through changes in adult born neurons. This possibility could be
assessed by blocking adult neurogenesis in the MG-Alk5-iKO during the behavioral testing
window.
- We now report that microglia morphology and pSMAD3 signal recover in the MG-Alk5
iKO mice (New Supplemental Fig 3), which is accompanied by reversal of the
neurogenesis phenotype and recovery (Fig 2) in both EPM/EZM and BM behavioral
phenotypes (Fig 10). Conversely, MG-Tgfb1 iKO microglia do not recover (New
Supplemental Fig 6), and the increase in neurogenesis in Tgfb1 is sustained for at least 12
weeks (New Supplemental Fig 5), which is accompanied by consistent behavioral
phenotypes at this time point (Fig 10). This supports the causal contribution of microglia
to neurogenesis phenotype and behavioral outcome. It is technically challenging to
specifically block neurogenesis without affecting the microglia phenotype in our mouse
model because microglia undergo cell division in iKO mice. Therefore, any agents that
target proliferating cells would also affect microglia phenotype in the iKO mice. We also
tested retroviral targeting of NSCs in HC in our microglial iKO mice; however, the
transduction efficiency is low, and the intracerebral injection activated microglia in the
hippocampus, which introduces additional confounds. Therefore, we are not confident
that intracerebral injection of anti-mitotic agents or retroviral-mediated DREADDs
inhibition will be ideal methods for directly testing this.
7. The cell count data are presented per section or per image field. This type of analysis can lead
to inaccurate comparisons if the brain regions of different treatment groups differ in size/volume.
The data should be presented as overall counts in a given brain region or as cell densities
(number of cells per volume).
- We apologize for this misrepresentation. For DG, we pick 6 brain sections at the same
anterior/posterior location where DG has a similar shape and length, and the cell count
for DCX+ cells is normalized to DG length. This is now reflected in revised figures.
Microglia and astrocyte counts were normalized to volume using unbiased stereological
counts.
8. The n size varies greatly across experiments. What is the justification for this? In cases where
just 3 mice are analyzed, it is questionable whether reliable results will be obtained. Also, some
of the data are presented with points representing individual cells. This is misleading and the
data should be shown as points for individual mice.
- Most experiments have a sample size of at least 4 and animals from at least two different
litters, which already reached statistical significance. For behavioral tests, we calculated
n based on the pilot study and power calculation. The only figure that labels individual
cells is Figures 6G and 6H, with the intention to show the distribution of microglia in
each mouse. However, the statistical analysis was carried out with the average from each
animal as a single n (this is now clearly stated in figure legend and raw data file). DCX+
cells were presented as the average from each animal as a single data point, which also
shows statistical significance since the phenotype is very robust. We have now calculated
the effect size for Figure 6 (with a large effect size; Cohen’s d=8.755227 and coefficient
r=0.9748874 for 6I and Cohen’s d=5.4435 and coefficient r=0.9386 for 6J). Nevertheless,
we now also pointed out the limitation of the small sample size in the revised manuscript.
9. The distribution of males and females is not even across the studies. Did the authors
investigate whether trends toward sex differences exist? If not, it is difficult to compare across
measures when some of them have with mixed sex mice and others have only one sex (e.g.,
Figure 4H).
- We did not observe an overt sex effect on our phenotype, consistent with the previous
report of a lack of sex effects on hippocampal adult neurogenesis (PMID: 18003841) or
our previous study on microglia in the TGF-β signaling-deficient mice (PMID:
38906887). Most experiments have both sexes, with the only exception being Figure 4H.
We have acknowledged that our study is not intended or powered to analyze sex
differences in the discussion.
10. Avoidance behavior on the EPM has been linked to ventral hippocampus, not dorsal
hippocampus. The images are all from dorsal hippocampus and it is not clear whether the entire
hippocampus was analyzed or just the dorsal part. Ventral hippocampus should be included.
- We have now included analysis of the ventral hippocampus, and data show that the
ventral hippocampus has increased DCX+ cells and dendrite arborization at 3 weeks but
not at 6 weeks or 12 weeks after TAM treatment, consistent with results from the dorsal
hippocampus (New supplementary Figure 2). Clarification on the analyzed hippocampal
region has been added to the figures.
11. Terms like "microglial activation," "dyshomeostasis," and "reactivity" are used
interchangeably. Consider defining and using them more consistently for clarity. It is not clear at
all what microglial dyshomeostasis is. Unless there is something different from microglial
reactivity, it should be eliminated from the text. If there is something different, it should be
defined as such.
- We have now changed it to either reactive microglia or TGF-β-deficient microglia.
Thank you for the suggestion.
12. The authors note that increased adult neurogenesis is transient (DCX+ peaks at 3 weeks).
Discussion on whether this reflects compensatory regulatory feedback, or microglia reversion to
a homeostatic state might be helpful. Whether changes in neurogenesis correlate with sustained
changes in microglial profile (e.g., do activated microglia persist at 6–12 weeks?).
- We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Please see the response to
Reviewer 1's comment #1 regarding the recovery of the microglia profile.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is
part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide
appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
- Thank you for providing valuable comments and suggestions for our manuscript.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript investigates the consequences of microglia-specific TGF-β signaling inhibition
on hippocampal adult neurogenesis and behavior. Using multiple inducible knockout models
(targeting TGF-β1, ALK5, and TβRII), the authors demonstrate that loss of microglial
homeostatic signaling leads to a transient increase in SGZ neurogenesis and a lasting increase in
mature neurons. Single-cell RNA sequencing and pharmacological inhibition experiments
support a mechanistic link via downregulation of PTEN and upregulation of the mTOR pathway
in neuroblasts. Behavioral testing indicates reduced anxiety-like behavior but no alteration in
forgetting.
This work is conceptually innovative, methodologically rigorous, and highly relevant for the
fields of neurogenesis, microglia-neuron crosstalk, and neuroinflammation. However,
clarification and strengthening of mechanistic interpretation, figure presentation, and behavioral
conclusions would improve the manuscript.
Major Comments
1. The finding that activated microglia can stimulate, rather than inhibit, adult neurogenesis in
the absence of injury contradicts longstanding assumptions and presents a paradigm shift.
- We thank Reviewer 4 for their positive comments and for acknowledging the novelty and
significance of our study.
2. The integration of transcriptomic and behavioral data makes this study of broad relevance to
neuroscience and regenerative biology.
- We thank Reviewer 4 for their positive comments and for acknowledging the potential
broad significance of our study.
3. The authors argue that the observed transient increase in DCX+ neuroblasts results in a long-
term gain in mature neurons. While this is supported by BrdU/NeuN data, the term "transient"
may be misleading. Please clarify this distinction and emphasize that the transient increase
refers to proliferation/differentiation, not integration.
- We have now revised the manuscript to reflect that the increase in DCX+ is in a cohort of
newly born neuroblasts, which later matured into neurons and integrated into the
circuitry.
4.The PTEN-mTOR link is well-supported; however, the authors should discuss whether other
converging pathways from their DEG data (e.g., synaptic organization, apoptotic signaling)
might also contribute.
- We have added a discussion to address this comment (page 26).
5. Behavioral phenotypes (reduced anxiety-like behavior and spatial learning deficits) are
presented as consequences of increased neurogenesis. However, causality remains correlative.
While the authors acknowledge limitations, the discussion would benefit from more elaboration
on future strategies to test this directly (e.g., combining NSC-targeted inhibition with microglial
KO background).
- We acknowledge this limitation due to technical challenges to target NSCs in our mouse
model without affecting proliferating microglia. We have now expanded the discussion
on this limitation and added a discussion on future strategies to test this directly (in
“Limitation of our study” at the end of the discussion).
6. The fear-conditioning “forgetting” paradigm might not be ideally timed. Consider clarifying
whether pre-treatment with TAM would be more suitable to test the influence of neurogenesis on
memory clearance.
- We agree with the reviewer, and to keep the focus of the current study, we have now
removed this data.
7. The Barnes Maze was used to assess spatial learning, but reversal learning—a component of
cognitive flexibility strongly linked to adult hippocampal neurogenesis—was not tested. Given
prior work by Kempermann and others demonstrating that reversal learning in tasks like the
Morris Water Maze is sensitive to neurogenesis status, the authors should briefly discuss this
limitation or provide justification for the behavioral test battery selected.
- We agree with the reviewer on this point. In our hands, reversal learning does not work
well with the Barnes Maze, potentially due to the long-time course needed to train mice
on this task and the less robust motivation (unlike the water maze, we use mild aversive
conditions, such as light and an overhead fan to motivate animals to find the target hole)
Mice usually are not motivated to find target hole in the later days of the reverse learning
phase of the test. We chose BM as a general learning/memory test to be consistent with
our previously published study (PMID: 38906887) to compare the results in Alk5 and
Tgfb1 iKO mice. We have added a discussion to acknowledge this limitation (pages 27-
28).
8. The scRNA-seq data are rich, but dense. Please consider a summary table or schematic of key
pathway-level changes (PTEN/mTOR, IGF1, TNF-α) for clarity.
- We have now revised the scRNA-seq figure. Key pathway changes are included in the
Supplementary data tables and Figure 7 M, N.
9. Improve visual clarity of UMAPs and volcano plots (Figure 7), including font sizes, axis
labels, and color keys.
- We have now revised the scRNAseq figure to increase the size of plots to improve visual
clarity and moved the PTEN-mTOR data into a new figure.
10. Some experiments (e.g., PLX5622 repopulation) use n=3–4 animals. These data should be
interpreted cautiously, and limitations of statistical power noted.
- We have added a sentence in the result section to note the low n number in this
experiment.
11. Sex as a variable and tamoxifen effects: The inclusion of both sexes and annotation of data
points by sex across figures is commendable. However, no sex-specific analysis is reported. If the
study was not powered or intended to detect sex differences, please state this explicitly in the
Methods or Discussion sections.
- This has been added to the discussion section.
Additionally, tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), and estrogen
signaling differs between males and females—particularly in the hippocampus where it
influences both neurogenesis and microglial function. Although tamoxifen is used here solely for
Cre activation, the potential for sex-dependent off-target effects should be acknowledged,
especially when interpreting behavioral and neurogenic outcomes.
- We acknowledge the effects of TAM on potential sex-dependent off-target effects;
however, we use control mice that are also subjected to the same TAM treatment to
minimize these effects. Our previous study has also shown that TAM treatment itself does
not cause behavior phenotype in Control (Cx3cr1CreER non floxed) mice (PMID:
38906887).
Minor Comments
12. Figure 7K–N: Highlight DCX+ cells migrating out of SGZ more clearly with arrows or
labels.
- Thank you for the suggestion. Migrated DCX+ cells are now marked by an arrowhead in
the figure.
13. Clarify whether the scRNA-seq was done on the whole hippocampus or DG-specific regions.
- scRNAseq was done on the whole hippocampus. This is now clarified in the method
section.
14. Refer consistently to “dyshomeostatic microglia” or “TGF-β-deficient microglia” rather
than broadly as “activated microglia.”
- We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. Based on this suggestion and that of Reviewer
#2, we have now changed it to either reactive microglia or TGF-β-deficient microglia.
